text: Russia spans 11 time zones — when it's 9am in Kaliningrad, it's already 8pm in Kamchatka 🕰️
The Mongol Empire covered ~23 million km² at its peak — the largest contiguous land empire in history. Roughly 16% of Earth's land, ruled from horseback.
More than half of the Netherlands sits less than 1 metre above sea level — and about a quarter is below it.
Canada has more lakes than the rest of the world combined.
The British Empire at its 1920 peak covered about 24% of Earth's land area. 'The empire on which the sun never sets' was not a metaphor.
Monaco is smaller than Central Park in New York (2.1 km² vs 3.4 km²).
Africa is bigger than China, India, the USA and most of Europe combined — Mercator maps just refuse to show it.
The Trans-Siberian Railway runs 9,289 km from Moscow to Vladivostok — the longest railway line on Earth.
Istanbul is the only major city that sits on two continents — and it served as an imperial capital for over 1,500 years.
In 1900, roughly 25% of the world's population lived in Europe. Today it's under 10%.
Vatican City is the smallest country on Earth (0.44 km²) — and its Swiss Guard, founded in 1506, is older than most modern states.
Russia sold Alaska to the US in 1867 for $7.2 million — about 2 cents per acre.
The Louisiana Purchase (1803) doubled the size of the United States overnight, at roughly 3 cents an acre.
The Ottoman Empire lasted 623 years (1299–1922) — longer than the entire history of most modern nations.
The shortest war in recorded history: Britain vs Zanzibar, 1896. Duration: about 38 minutes.
France was still executing people by guillotine when Star Wars premiered. The last use was in 1977.
Germany made its final WWI reparations payment in October 2010 — 92 years after the war ended.
About 90% of the world's population lives in the Northern Hemisphere.
The Sahara is roughly the size of the United States — and it was green savanna with lakes and hippos just 6,000 years ago.
Indonesia is made up of over 17,000 islands and stretches wider than the continental United States.
The Danube flows through or borders 10 countries — more than any other river on Earth.
Mount Everest grows about 4 mm taller every year as the Indian plate keeps pushing into Asia.
The Dead Sea shore sits about 430 m below sea level — the lowest dry land on Earth — and keeps dropping every year.
44 countries have no coastline. Two are double-landlocked (you must cross TWO countries to reach the sea): Liechtenstein and Uzbekistan.
The Berlin Wall stood for 10,316 days. As of 2018, it has been gone longer than it ever stood.
China used more cement in 2011–2013 than the United States used in the entire 20th century.
All the walls built across Chinese dynasties total roughly 21,000 km — about half the Earth's circumference.
At the Cold War's peak in 1986, the world held ~70,000 nuclear warheads. Today: ~12,000.
The 1918 flu pandemic killed more people in 6 months than WWI did in 4 years.
Roman harbor concrete has survived 2,000 years of seawater. Modern marine concrete is designed to last decades.
The Mongol conquests may have depopulated so much farmland that regrowing forests measurably cooled the planet.
When the Spanish arrived in 1519, Tenochtitlan was larger than almost any city in Europe — built on a lake, connected by causeways.
The Soviet Union covered one-sixth of Earth's land surface.
Brazil borders every country in South America except Chile and Ecuador.
Africa has 54 countries — more than a quarter of all UN member states — and a median age of just 19.
More than a third of humanity lives in just two countries: India and China.
Kazakhstan is the world's largest landlocked country — bigger than all of Western Europe.
Rome's road network reached ~80,000 km of paved highways — enough to circle the Earth twice.
When the Great Pyramid of Giza was built, woolly mammoths still lived on Wrangel Island. They survived until ~1650 BC.
Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire. Teaching began at Oxford around 1096; Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325.
World population reached 1 billion around 1804. It took 123 years to add the second billion — and just 12 years to add the eighth.
Sweden has not fought a war since 1814 — over two centuries of unbroken peace.
There are over 7,000 languages on Earth — but half of humanity speaks just 23 of them.
You can ski on the equator: the Cayambe volcano in Ecuador carries glaciers right on the line.
The Netherlands is the world's #2 agricultural exporter by value — from a country you can drive across in 3 hours.
Historians estimate Mansa Musa of Mali may have been the richest person in history — his gold spending on one pilgrimage disrupted Cairo's economy for years (1324).
The Suez Canal cuts ~7,000 km off the Europe–Asia sea route. Roughly 12% of global trade passes through it.
The Panama Canal saves ships a ~13,000 km detour around Cape Horn.
Greenland is the world's largest island — 80% of it lies under an ice sheet up to 3 km thick.
The Black Death killed an estimated 30–60% of Europe's population in just 4 years (1347–1351). Survivors' wages rose so fast that governments passed laws to cap them.
The Inca Empire ran ~40,000 km of roads through the Andes — without wheels, iron tools, or a writing system.
The 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora caused the 'Year Without a Summer' — snow fell on New England in June 1816, and harvests failed across Europe.
Antarctica is the largest desert on Earth — far bigger than the Sahara.
In 1914, one US dollar bought 4.2 German marks. By November 1923, it bought 4.2 trillion.
The Great Emu War of 1932: Australia deployed soldiers with machine guns against emus. The emus won.
Portugal and England have the world's oldest active alliance — signed in 1373 and still in force.
Ethiopia follows a calendar roughly 7 years behind the rest of the world — and clocks that start counting from dawn.
About 71% of Earth is ocean — but humans have mapped the surface of Mars in more detail than the ocean floor.
Point Nemo, the spot in the Pacific farthest from any land, is so remote that the nearest humans are often the astronauts passing overhead on the ISS.
Australia is wider than the Moon — about 4,000 km across, versus the Moon's roughly 3,475 km diameter.
Chile is about 4,300 km long but on average only ~180 km wide. Flipped on its side, it would stretch from Lisbon past Moscow.
The Caspian Sea is the world's largest lake — bigger than Germany.
Lake Baikal in Siberia holds roughly 20% of the world's unfrozen fresh water, and at ~1,642 m it's the deepest lake on Earth.
The Amazon River pushes about one-fifth of all the river water on Earth into the ocean — more than the next several biggest rivers combined.
The Mariana Trench is deeper than Mount Everest is tall — drop Everest in and its peak would still sit about 2 km underwater.
Iceland has essentially no mosquitoes — one of the very few inhabited places on Earth without them.
Counting its fjords and islands, Norway's coastline runs roughly 100,000 km — enough to circle the Earth about two and a half times.
Africa is the only continent that sits in all four hemispheres: north, south, east and west.
The equator passes through 13 countries — and in Quito, Ecuador, you can stand with one foot in each hemisphere at ~2,850 m altitude.
Alaska is both the westernmost AND easternmost US state: the Aleutian Islands cross the 180° meridian.
The closest US state to Africa isn't Florida — it's Maine, whose eastern tip sits nearer to Morocco than Miami does.
Reno, Nevada is farther west than Los Angeles, California. Check a map — the coastline bends hard.
At the Strait of Gibraltar, Africa and Europe are only about 14 km apart — on a clear day you can see one continent from the other.
Russia and the US are less than 4 km apart. Between the Diomede Islands in the Bering Strait, the date line makes them ~21 hours apart — locals call them Tomorrow Island and Yesterday Isle.
Finland has an estimated 188,000 lakes — roughly one for every 30 Finns.
The Sargasso Sea is the only sea on Earth with no coastline — it's bounded entirely by ocean currents.
Landlocked Bolivia still maintains a navy of several thousand personnel — patrolling Lake Titicaca and waiting to reclaim the coastline it lost to Chile in 1884.
Everest is the highest point above sea level, but the summit of Ecuador's Chimborazo is the farthest point from the Earth's center — the planet bulges at the equator.
Angel Falls in Venezuela drops 979 m — roughly 15 times the height of Niagara.
Every point in Lesotho lies above 1,400 m — the highest 'low point' of any country on Earth.
The highest natural point of the Maldives is about 2.4 m above sea level — the lowest 'high point' of any country.
Bir Tawil, a patch of desert between Egypt and Sudan, is claimed by neither country — one of the only unclaimed pieces of land on Earth.
The Belgian-Dutch border town of Baarle is a puzzle of 30+ enclaves — the frontier runs through houses and cafés, and your tax residence could depend on where your front door is.
The Pacific Ocean is larger than every piece of land on Earth combined.
Sailors' trivia: the longest straight-line ocean voyage on Earth runs roughly 32,000 km from Pakistan to Kamchatka — without touching land.
The Atlantic Ocean widens by roughly 2-3 cm every year — about the speed your fingernails grow. Columbus's voyage is over a metre longer today.
Measured from its underwater base, Hawaii's Mauna Kea is taller than Everest — over 10,000 m from seabed to summit.
Antarctica holds an estimated 60-70% of all the fresh water on Earth — locked in ice up to 4.8 km thick.
France spans 12 time zones — more than any other country — thanks to territories from French Polynesia to the Caribbean.
China, nearly as wide as the continental US, uses a single time zone. In the far west, the sun can set close to midnight Beijing time.
Spain has been in the 'wrong' time zone since 1940, when Franco moved clocks to Berlin time. Geographically, Madrid should share a zone with London.
Nepal's clocks are set to UTC+5:45 — one of only a handful of 45-minute time zones on Earth.
An estimated 27 million tonnes of Saharan dust blows across the Atlantic each year — and fertilizes the Amazon rainforest with phosphorus.
The Great Barrier Reef is the largest structure ever built by living creatures — about 2,300 km long and visible from orbit.
Lake Titicaca, at ~3,800 m, is the highest lake in the world with large-scale commercial navigation.
The Kaliningrad region — home to a million Russians — has no land connection to Russia. It's the old East Prussia, taken in 1945.
Mount Thor on Canada's Baffin Island has Earth's greatest vertical drop: 1,250 m of pure cliff.
About 40% of the world's population lives within 100 km of a coastline.
The US has at least nine towns named Rome, several Parises, Athenses and Moscows — 19th-century settlers named frontier towns after the great cities they hoped to rival.
The Andes are the longest mountain range on land: ~7,000 km through 7 countries.
Damascus and Jericho both claim to be the oldest continuously inhabited city on Earth — each with evidence stretching back roughly 10,000 years.
The Sahara isn't the biggest desert on Earth — both Antarctica and the Arctic are larger. It's just the biggest HOT one.
Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid — the pyramid was already ~2,500 years old when she was born.
Harvard was founded before calculus existed. The university opened in 1636; Newton and Leibniz published calculus decades later.
Nintendo was founded in 1889 — while the Ottoman Empire still ruled the Middle East and the Eiffel Tower was brand new. It made playing cards.
The fax machine was patented in 1843 — 33 years before the telephone, while wagon trains were still crossing the Oregon Trail.
The London Underground opened in 1863 — before Germany or Italy existed as unified countries.
The United States paid its last Civil War pension in 2020 — Irene Triplett, daughter of a Confederate-turned-Union soldier, collected $73.13 a month until she died.
President John Tyler was born in 1790, when George Washington was president. Astonishingly, one of his grandsons was still alive in the 2020s — two generations spanning 230+ years.
Anne Frank, Martin Luther King Jr. and Audrey Hepburn were all born in the same year: 1929.
The Hundred Years' War actually lasted 116 years (1337-1453). The name stuck anyway.
The Netherlands and the Isles of Scilly were technically at war for 335 years (1651-1986) without a single shot fired. Peace was finally signed in 1986, mostly for fun.
Rome and Carthage formally ended the Third Punic War in 1985 — when the mayors of the two cities signed a symbolic peace treaty, 2,131 years after the fighting stopped.
Genetic studies suggest roughly 1 in 200 men alive today may descend from Genghis Khan's male line — an estimated 16 million descendants.
The Great Fire of London in 1666 destroyed ~13,000 houses and 87 churches — yet the official recorded death toll was in single digits. Historians suspect many deaths simply went unrecorded.
The oldest known customer complaint is ~3,770 years old: a Babylonian tablet from one Nanni, furious at the merchant Ea-nasir over substandard copper.
Göbekli Tepe in Turkey is roughly 6,000 years older than Stonehenge — monumental architecture built by people who hadn't yet invented pottery or farming.
Ancient Romans were already tourists at the pyramids — graffiti from Roman visitors survives inside them.
The Roman Empire (in the East) fell just 39 years before Columbus sailed. Constantinople fell in 1453; the Americas were reached in 1492.
Napoleon wasn't short. At ~1.68 m (5'7") he was average or above for a Frenchman of his era — the myth came from British propaganda and French inches.
The Eiffel Tower was supposed to be demolished after 20 years — it was saved because it made a good radio antenna.
The Eiffel Tower grows roughly 15 cm taller on hot summer days as the iron expands.
The Statue of Liberty operated as an official lighthouse from 1886 to 1902.
'Big Ben' is the bell, not the tower. The tower is officially the Elizabeth Tower.
The Leaning Tower of Pisa took about 200 years to finish — and it was already leaning before builders reached the top. They built the upper floors at an angle to compensate.
Ancient sources claim the Colosseum was flooded for staged naval battles — full-size ships, in the middle of Rome.
Vikings reached North America around the year 1000 — nearly five centuries before Columbus. The site at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland is a UNESCO site.
Iceland's parliament, the Althing, first met in 930 AD — making it arguably the oldest surviving parliament on Earth.
San Marino, founded (by tradition) in 301 AD, claims to be the world's oldest republic — and it made Abraham Lincoln an honorary citizen in 1861. He wrote back thanking them.
At the 1936 Olympics, Liechtenstein and Haiti discovered they had identical flags. Liechtenstein added a crown the next year.
In 2007, ~170 Swiss soldiers accidentally invaded Liechtenstein after getting lost in the dark. Liechtenstein, which has no army, didn't notice.
Lady Jane Grey ruled England for just nine days in 1553 — probably the shortest confirmed reign in the country's history.
In September 1914, the French army rushed ~5,000 soldiers to the Battle of the Marne in commandeered Paris taxis.
On Christmas 1914, German and British soldiers climbed out of the trenches, exchanged gifts, sang carols and played football in no-man's-land. Commanders made sure it never happened again.
Kongō Gumi, a Japanese temple-building firm founded in 578 AD, operated independently for over 1,400 years — the oldest company in recorded history.
For over 200 years (1639-1853), Japan sealed itself off almost completely — foreign trade limited mostly to one small artificial island in Nagasaki harbor.
The Great Wall of China is NOT visible from the Moon — and astronauts report it's barely visible even from low orbit.
The Terracotta Army guarding Qin Shi Huang's tomb has ~8,000 soldiers — and no two faces are alike.
The Library of Alexandria wasn't destroyed in one great fire — it declined over centuries of budget cuts, purges and neglect. The boring version is the true one.
The Aztec Empire was younger than Oxford University — it lasted less than a century (1428-1521) before Cortés arrived.
Machu Picchu was built around 1450 and abandoned only ~100 years later. The Spanish never found it — which is why it survived.
Timbuktu's families and libraries preserved an estimated 350,000+ medieval manuscripts — proof of a golden age of African scholarship centered on a city Europeans dismissed as legend.
Ethiopia is the only African country never colonized by a European power — Italy occupied it for just 5 years (1936-41) and never subdued it.
Haiti became the first Black republic in 1804 after the only successful slave revolution in history — then France forced it to pay 'compensation' to former slaveholders until 1947.
The US bought the Virgin Islands from Denmark in 1917 for $25 million in gold.
Sweden's Vasa warship sank in 1628, twenty minutes into its maiden voyage, in full view of the crowd. Raised in 1961, it's now the world's best-preserved 17th-century ship.
The Antikythera mechanism, recovered from a Greek shipwreck, is a ~2,100-year-old geared device that predicted eclipses and planetary positions — an ancient analog computer.
Passenger flight has gotten slower: Concorde crossed New York-London in under 3.5 hours. It retired in 2003, and nothing has replaced it.
The Apollo 11 guidance computer had less processing power than a modern washing machine. It still navigated to the Moon and back.
The Soviet Union lost roughly 27 million people in WW2 — about 1 in 7 of its entire population.
The Zimmermann Telegram — Germany secretly offering Mexico the return of Texas, New Mexico and Arizona — was intercepted by the British and helped push the US into WWI in 1917.

In 1943, British intelligence dressed a corpse as a Royal Marines officer, gave it fake invasion plans, and floated it to a Spanish beach. Hitler moved divisions to Greece; the Allies landed in Sicily.
The US 'Ghost Army' of WW2 was ~1,100 artists and engineers with inflatable tanks and sound trucks — they impersonated entire divisions and fooled German intelligence repeatedly.
Witold Pilecki volunteered to be imprisoned in Auschwitz. He spent 2.5 years inside organizing resistance and smuggling out the first reports of the Holocaust, then escaped.
Japanese officer Hiroo Onoda kept fighting WW2 in the Philippine jungle until 1974 — 29 years after the surrender. He gave up only when his long-retired former commander flew out to order him home.
At the peak of the Berlin Airlift, an Allied supply plane landed in West Berlin roughly every 45 seconds — for over a year, an entire city of 2 million fed entirely by air.
The Code of Hammurabi (~1750 BC) is one of the oldest surviving law codes — nearly 300 laws carved in stone, including the original 'eye for an eye.'
Persia's Royal Road let royal messengers cover ~2,700 km in about a week — and Herodotus's praise of those couriers ('neither snow nor rain...') became the US Postal Service motto.
Tsar Peter the Great taxed beards — Russian nobles had to carry a token proving they'd paid for the right to keep theirs.
Before 1917, Russia's calendar ran 13 days behind Western Europe — which is why the 'October Revolution' happened in November.
Britain and its colonies skipped 11 days in 1752 when switching calendars: September 2 was followed directly by September 14.
Legend has it Russia's shooting team missed the 1908 London Olympics by arriving 12 days late — the empire still ran on the old Julian calendar.
The guillotine was proposed as a humanitarian reform — Dr. Guillotin wanted executions to be equal and painless. He didn't invent it and hated that it bore his name.
When Genghis Khan died in 1227, the escort reportedly killed everyone it met on the way to his burial — and his grave has never been found to this day.
The Byzantine Empire never called itself 'Byzantine' — its citizens called themselves Romans right up to 1453. The name was invented by historians a century after it fell.

Spain's Council of the Indies governed an empire on which the sun literally never set — Philip II ruled territory in Europe, the Americas, Africa and Asia by the 1580s, three centuries before the British claimed the phrase.
The world's first paper money appeared in Song-dynasty China around the 11th century — Marco Polo's reports of it were dismissed in Europe as fantasy.
Venice's Republic lasted 1,100 years (697-1797) — longer than the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire in the West combined.
The Pony Express, icon of the American West, operated for just 18 months before the telegraph killed it.
Ancient Egyptian workers on royal tombs staged the first recorded labor strike in history (~1157 BC) — they downed tools when grain rations ran late.
Roman gladiators rarely fought to the death — they were expensive investments, and sweat scraped from their skin was sold as a cosmetic.
Charlemagne, crowned in 800, is a documented ancestor of essentially every living person with European ancestry — genealogy's math makes it nearly unavoidable.
Ukraine now spends roughly 40% of its GDP on defense, per Our World in Data (SIPRI) — a war burden no other country today comes close to matching.
The world's biggest meat eaters per person aren't Americans: Tonga tops the map at roughly 157 kg per person per year, per Our World in Data.
Romania drinks more than anywhere on Earth: about 16.8 litres of pure alcohol per person per year, per Our World in Data.
France receives roughly 100 million international tourists a year — more than its entire population, per Our World in Data.
In Norway, about 9 in 10 new cars sold are electric. In the US, it's roughly 1 in 10, per Our World in Data.
Half of Niger's population is younger than 15. Half of Japan's is older than 49. Two opposite demographic worlds, one planet, per Our World in Data.
Monaco packs about 19,000 people into every square kilometre. Mongolia has about 2, per Our World in Data.
The US spends about 17% of its GDP on healthcare — a larger share than any nation in recorded history, per Our World in Data.
Israel and South Korea invest roughly 5% of GDP in research and development — most countries manage under 1%, per Our World in Data.
Suriname is about 97% forest — the most forested country on Earth. Iceland: under 1%, per Our World in Data.
Cuba and much of Europe have 4+ doctors per 1,000 people. Parts of Africa have fewer than 0.1, per Our World in Data.
Japan and South Korea have 10+ hospital beds per 1,000 people — several times the level of the US or UK, per Our World in Data.
The US and El Salvador imprison more people per capita than anywhere else on Earth, per Our World in Data.
Extreme poverty (under $2.15/day) is now concentrated almost entirely in one region: Sub-Saharan Africa, per Our World in Data. In 1990, most of the world's poorest lived in Asia.
Global literacy has passed 87% — but in parts of the Sahel, fewer than half of adults can read, per Our World in Data.
Workers in Cambodia and Mexico log 2,200+ hours a year. Germans work about 1,300 — the equivalent of ~5 months less, per Our World in Data.
Half of Earth's habitable land is used for agriculture — and most of that feeds livestock, not people directly, per Our World in Data.
Iceland gets about 80% of its energy from low-carbon sources — the highest share of any country, per Our World in Data.
In 1950 the average woman worldwide had about 5 children. Today it's roughly 2.2 — the fastest reproductive shift in human history, per Our World in Data.
South Korea's fertility rate is about 0.7 births per woman. At that rate, 100 Koreans have ~33 children and ~11 grandchildren.
Most countries now have more mobile phone subscriptions than people, per Our World in Data.
Global life expectancy is now about 73 years. In 1900 it was roughly 32 — humanity has more than doubled its lifespan in five generations, per Our World in Data.
A century ago, about 1 in 4 children worldwide died before their fifth birthday. Today it's under 1 in 25 — still too many, but a 90% fall, per Our World in Data.
Some Gulf states emit more CO2 per person than the US — and many times the global average, per Our World in Data.
Northern Europeans drink more milk than anyone on Earth — Finland tops most rankings. Much of East Asia consumes almost none, per Our World in Data.
Malaria still kills hundreds of thousands of people a year — and the deaths are now almost entirely concentrated in Africa, per Our World in Data.
Japan has nearly one retiree for every two working-age people. In much of Africa the ratio is closer to one per twenty, per Our World in Data.
Nature's constant: about 105 boys are born for every 100 girls, almost everywhere on Earth. Countries far above that line have a story to explain, per Our World in Data.
In some Pacific island nations, more than half of all adults are obese — the highest rates on Earth, per Our World in Data.
Bahrain, Kuwait, Monaco and Singapore are effectively 100% urban. Much of East Africa is still mostly rural, per Our World in Data.
Papua New Guinea has roughly 840 living languages — more than any other country, in a population smaller than London's.
Basque, spoken in the Pyrenees, has no known living relatives — it likely predates the arrival of Indo-European languages in Europe by thousands of years.
English is an official or primary language in ~60 sovereign states — more than any other language. The UK itself has no law making it official.
More people speak English in total than any other language — but Mandarin and Spanish both have more NATIVE speakers.
At least part of the Bible has been translated into over 3,500 languages — the complete text into 700+.
Zimbabwe recognizes 16 official languages — the most of any country.
Switzerland has four national languages — and a fifth unofficial one, English, increasingly used between the other four.
Icelandic has changed so little in 800 years that modern Icelanders can still read the medieval sagas in the original.
The Hawaiian alphabet has just 13 letters. The Khmer script of Cambodia has 74 characters — the world's longest alphabet.
The Rotokas language of Papua New Guinea uses an alphabet of only 12 letters — the world's shortest.
The British pound is the world's oldest currency still in use — its origins go back roughly 1,200 years.
The word 'salary' may come from Roman soldiers' salt allowance — 'salarium.' Even Pliny the Elder repeated the story, though historians still argue about it.
Nepal has the only national flag that isn't a rectangle — two stacked pennants, representing the Himalaya.
Only two countries have square flags: Switzerland and the Vatican.
Denmark's flag, by legend falling from the sky in 1219, is the oldest continuously used national flag on Earth.
Tyrian purple, the dye of Roman emperors, was extracted from sea snails — thousands of snails per gram, making it worth more than gold.
Ethiopia's Ge'ez script has been in continuous use for over 2,000 years — one of the oldest alphabets still written daily.
The Cherokee syllabary was invented in the 1820s by Sequoyah, who couldn't read any language — within years, Cherokee literacy rates surpassed those of their English-speaking neighbors.
There are more possible chess games than atoms in the observable universe — chess arrived in Europe ~1,000 years ago via Persia and the Arab world, from India.
Oktoberfest mostly takes place in September.
The croissant isn't French — it descends from the Austrian kipferl, brought to Paris in the 1830s by a Viennese baker.
Fortune cookies were invented in California, most likely by Japanese immigrants. They're almost unknown in China.
Vanilla is native to Mexico — for 300 years the Aztecs' secret ingredient in chocolate. Most 'vanilla' flavor today is synthetic.
The Ottoman Empire had a state department of tulips — the flower that triggered Dutch 'tulip mania' came to Europe from Istanbul, not Amsterdam.
